# The War of the Iron Lilypads

Gather close, young ones, and I'll tell you how the Great Marsh came to be.

Long ago, before your great-great-grandparents grew their legs, the toads lived scattered and afraid. The herons ruled from above with their sharp beaks. The snapping turtles claimed the deep waters as their own, demanding tribute of the tastiest flies. The toads? They hid in mud, each pond to itself, weak and divided.

Then came the Cattail Engineers.

Old Croaker didn't have a crown. No one voted for her. She simply *was*—the one who knew how to weave floating roots into bridges. Others gathered. Not because they had to. Because they wanted to cross.

She taught young toads to build. They taught others. No one owned the knowledge. It spread like ripples.

When the herons grew bold and the turtles sent their armored soldiers, the toads faced their darkest hour. But they had no war-chief to capture. No palace to burn. The Cattail Engineers had built *everywhere*—a thousand lilypads, each a fortress, each connected by root-bridges that only toads could traverse.

The herons struck one pad. The toads simply... weren't there. They'd already scattered through tunnels of reed and root, reappearing behind the enemy, on pads the invaders couldn't reach. The turtles' heavy shells sank the lilies they climbed, while toads danced on edges too light to break.

The invaders exhausted themselves against a society with no center to destroy.

Afterward, something stranger happened. Victory didn't create kings. The Engineers kept building because building pleased them. The scouts kept watching because watching suited their temperaments. The singers composed new songs of the war—not to praise heroes, but to teach the tactics, so every tadpole would know.

You see how it works, young ones?

When the dry season comes and the pond shrinks, no one commands the migration. The old simply *go*, and the young follow, learning the paths. When a new threat appears, no one waits for orders. The nearest toad acts, and others join or not, as their judgment permits.

The Iron Lilypads rusted long ago. But the bridges remain, rebuilt countless times by toads who never met the original builders. The herons still circle, but they hunt elsewhere now—not from mercy, but from calculation. Toads are too troublesome, too dispersed, too *unpredictable* to rule.

Your tail will drop soon. Your legs will grow strong. You will choose what you become—hunter, builder, singer, scout, or something new we don't yet have words for. No one will assign you. No one *can*.

The pond has no master. Therefore, it has room for masters of every craft.

Sleep deep, dream of flying, and wake ready to leap.

*—Your Auntie, who builds dams when the mood takes her*
